extracted.intended_audience: high-school journalism students and student-newspaper staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing and managing a high‑school student newspaper: newsroom organization, roles and duties, copy preparation, diction/style rules, and page make‑up/layout principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite stories to improve them
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite the following stories in any way that will improve them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided leads and bodies; make bodies follow leads without awkward breaks; note whether leads were overstatements or understatements. (Exercise instruction — practical editing task.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead-body alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to make the bodies of the stories follow the leads without awkward breaks. Note whether the leads were overstatements or understatements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing, check that the lead's claim is supported by the body; revise lead or body to remove mismatch or misleading emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with printing-office terms
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the student familiarize himself with the following terms (add., bank/deck, B.F., box, break-line, catch-line/guide-line, chase, condensed/expanded type, copy, copy cutter, dead, display type, em, end mark, filler, flush, folo, form, galley, galley proof, hold, jump head, justifier, justify, kill, lead, lower/upper case, morgue, must, pi, pi line, quoins, rule, slug, solid, stick, stickful, stone, streamer/banner head, take).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorize definitions before studying make-up; know production marks and meanings (e.g., 'copy is clean' means needs little correction; 'hold' instructs not to print; 'must' marks essential copy). Understanding jargon aids correct production and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient staff organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficient organization of the editorial staff is the first requisite for success in putting out a school paper: every task must be assigned definitely to somebody, and everybody on the paper must have his regular duties, for the performance of which he — and he alone — is responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assigning duties to the staff in general (which leads to neglect). Prevent 'passing the buck' by clear accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit staff size and meaningful positions (no honorary editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unwise to have a large number of editors. Every staff title should mean something; when an editorship becomes 'honorary' it should be dropped from the mast head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make positions hard to win so they remain desirable; on small papers combine positions; on large papers subdivide work only if substantive. Avoid vague titles (e.g., 'literary editor') unless duties are clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor (editor-in-chief) responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor supervises the staff, makes recommendations for staff appointments and dismissals, decides questions of policy, advises sub-editors, passes upon availability of contributions, allots departmental space, and represents the paper officially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor is responsible to the faculty adviser and wields near-absolute authority provided there are no grave errors in conduct; need not write all editorials — management and supervision are primary duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate editor responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The associate editor usually writes most of the editorials and should be one of the best-informed workers on the staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must know school affairs thoroughly, have a large fund of general information, and be able to write live, convincing editorials. If the associate writes editorials, he should have little else to do and should not be overloaded with management details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up editor responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The make-up editor is responsible for the appearance of the paper: plans the arrangement of headings, directs the printer where to place each story, and (with advertising) supervises placement of ads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receive a copy schedule from the news editor and work out a balanced page make-up; headlines should be written to fit stories (stories never written to fit headlines); the make-up editor's work is technical and sometimes mechanical; ingenuity is often required.

rubrics_metrics.name: News editor responsibilities and 'play' decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The news editor is in charge at the copy desk, where matter is corrected, headed, and prepared for the typesetter; he marks stories with headline numbers and allocates 'play' (the prominence) for each article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story needs rewriting, cutting, or development, instruct copy readers accordingly. Confer with editor/school editor when in doubt. Enter heading number and estimated inches on the copy schedule and send prepared copy to the printer. It is essential that every story be scheduled — unscheduled copy may be overlooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: School editor duties (news gathering & assignment scheduling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The school editor gathers news tips, makes assignments, directs reporters, and keeps a 'future book' of tips to prepare weekly assignment schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create assignment schedules with story titles, reporter names, due dates, and returned dates; call reporters, advise on interviewing, stress important parts to cover, and check staff output to ensure required columns are filled. Hold reporters accountable for timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sporting editor duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The sporting editor leads sports writers, makes sports assignments, and is responsible for all sports stories; may correct/head his own copy and handle sport page make-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have an organized staff able to get play-by-play accounts; include a girl reporter when girls' teams exist; understand every form of sport and describe games fluently without eccentric slang.

rubrics_metrics.name: Club editor duties and anti-favoritism practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A club editor should handle stories of democratic clubs (not private social affairs) and rewrite club secretaries' notes into news form; group club reports under a general lead featuring outstanding weekly events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotate the order of club notices weekly to avoid giving long-term prominence to any one organization; club notices should be presented as news, not private social gossip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange editor standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The exchange editor reads exchange papers and conducts a column of news of other schools; his department should contain intelligent critical reviews and important news of other schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely clip jokes and editorials; occasionally reprint items with due credit; use the exchange page to make the paper interesting and to win friends in other schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor and feature editor standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The humor and feature writer should be original, impersonal, and clean-minded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Welcome contributions, seek comical occurrences and witty sayings, never 'crib' risqué witticisms from comic publications, avoid sarcasm and ridicule, and ask whether a personal joke is likely to hurt a student. Clean originality is essential; stale or cruel humor is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy readers and reporters: quality expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters supply news; copy readers correct and prepare copy for heading and typesetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy should be as 'clean' as possible (requiring little correction); the news editor and make-up editor rely on copy readers to produce publishable copy; follow later chapters for detailed methods of writing specific story types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines should fit stories
rubrics_metrics.description: On a properly edited paper headlines are written to fit stories; stories are never written to fit headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid manufacturing stories to justify a flashy headline; let headline size and wording reflect the actual story content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide pages/columns/typography before make-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Before undertaking publication editors must decide how many pages the paper shall contain, how many columns on a page, and how wide each column shall be; they must work out a complete schedule of headings and select type suitable for headings and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base these decisions on financial resources and the amount of interesting news available; copying a daily newspaper's make-up is discouraged — high-school events seldom justify daily‑paper headline sizes; conservatism should govern make-up choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Column width and type-size standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Column width and type-size recommendations for high‑school publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use average column width of 12.5 or 13 ems. For a four- or five-column paper, 18- or 24-point type is large enough for most important headings. In six- or seven-column papers use no larger than 30- or 36-point headings. Use 8-point Roman for body/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title and design: plain and readable
rubrics_metrics.description: For the name at the top of the first page use plain black letters rather than fanciful designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain black letters are easiest to read and look less amateurish; seek attractiveness and individuality without garishness or eccentricity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up editor page-priority and placement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles for placing stories and elements on the page: the most important position is upper right-hand corner of the first page, then upper left-hand corner, then parts of middle columns above the fold, then lower right/left corners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1. Place the leading story (top heading) in the upper right-hand corner. 2. Place the second most important story in the upper left-hand corner. 3. Middle columns above the fold follow in importance, then lower corners. 4. If a heavy headline is used, 'dress' the page toward the upper left to balance the top heading. 5. Cuts or cartoons should be placed at top (preferably) or bottom and balanced with headlines to avoid a 'lopsided' appearance. 6. Balance headlines for symmetry but avoid geometric plotting that makes a page look like a pattern. 7. Avoid placing headlines in adjoining columns next to each other — this weakens readability and appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrations/cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a cut or cartoon is used, place it at the top of the page preferably, or at the bottom, and 'balance' it carefully with headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the cut does not make the page lopsided; balance visual weight across columns and with surrounding headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and symmetry without formulaic plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: Care should be taken to balance headlines and the appearance of the page to make it symmetrical, but geometric plotting should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek visual balance and reader focus rather than rigid patterns; avoid making a page look like a dress-goods pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy scheduling and tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: The news editor enters heading number, top bank words, and approximate space (in inches) on the copy schedule, then turns the schedule over to the make-up editor; every story must be scheduled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a copy schedule to record all articles for an issue so the make-up editor can check material and prevent mislaid copy from being omitted. A 'dummy' page can be used but is unnecessary if the schedule is accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ornate/wordy diction — prefer plain expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Young writers should prefer the plainest and most direct expressions and avoid ornate or pretentious phrases. Specific prohibitions and correct alternatives are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of wrong vs right from the text: 'burglarize' (wrong) → 'a burglar broke into the house' or 'the house was robbed'; 'discourse sweet music' → 'play'; 'favored with a selection' → 'played a selection'; 'rendered a vocal solo' → 'sang a song'; 'specimen of humanity' → 'person'; 'the student body' → 'the students'; 'proud possessor' → 'owner/has'; 'those with whom we come in contact' → 'people we meet'; 'was the recipient of' → 'received'; 'wended their way' → 'went'; 'aggregate' → 'total'; 'consensus of opinion' → 'consensus'; 'casket' → 'coffin' when appropriate; 'commence' → 'begin'; 'destroyed by fire' → 'burned'; 'en route' → 'on the way'; 'conflagration' → 'fire'; 'individual' → 'person'; 'participate' → 'take part'; 'reside' → 'live'. Prefer concise, familiar words over ornate substitutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid euphemistic or inflated phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use inflated or trite phrases when simpler words suffice (examples: 'specimen of humanity', 'recipient of', 'wended their way').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace wordy/trite constructions with direct, specific alternatives to improve clarity and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor column ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The humor column must be original, clean-minded, and not at the expense of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never 'crib' material from low-quality comic publications; avoid risqué jokes, sarcasm, ridicule; evaluate whether a personal joke is likely to hurt a student before publishing.
